A person working on a project brings you a question about one part of it. The part is at the Address code.system.management.knowledge, and here is what the project's functional map holds about it: the element, what it receives and provides, and why.

# Metaform

## Metaform

`code.system.management.knowledge`, DE

Paths: src/metaform/__init__.py, artifacts/specs-draft/base-063-065-source-placement-removed-2026-10-15.md, specifications/01-map.md, README.md, src/metaform/modules/orchestration/specifications.py, src/metaform/modules/mcp/resources/prompts.xml, src/metaform/modules/workflow/runs.py, src/metaform/modules/workflow/__init__.py, src/metaform/modules/workflow/catalog.py, src/metaform/modules/dispatch/runner.py, src/metaform/modules/web/server.py, src/metaform/loader.py, src/metaform/modules/autoticket/watch.py, src/metaform/modules/web/__init__.py, src/metaform/modules/web/watchdog.py, src/metaform/modules/workflow/tests/test_ticket_runs.py, src/metaform/modules/web/tests/test_dispatch_settings.py, tests/test_module_combinations.py, src/metaform/modules/fork/repository.py, src/metaform/modules/fork/resources/template/__init__.py, specifications/04-chassis-modules.md, src/metaform/modules/web/providers.py, src/metaform/modules/mcp/views.py, src/metaform/modules/node/config.py, src/metaform/modules/dispatch/__init__.py, src/metaform/modules/fork/review.py, src/metaform/modules/mcp/view_manifest.py, scripts/hatch_views.py, src/metaform/module.py, src/metaform/module_metadata.py, src/metaform/relay.py, src/metaform/build.py

### Metaform receives from Jev

Asks typed decisions, caches answers and records actionable judgments at their addresses while preserving ordinary behavior when disabled or unavailable.

Why: Reuse typed judgments for agent allocation, knowledge ordering, triage, intake coverage and session diagnostics.

### Metaform receives from Web GUI

Serves live graph, node and layer views, source and memory inspection, work board, agent chat, attachments, diagrams, embedded apps, permissions, workspaces and build downloads.

Why: Let the person inspect the functional map and direct knowledge, work and agent activity from one persistent view.

### Metaform receives from twilio

Bridges authenticated calls and texts to the system agent and sends selected project notifications to configured owner numbers.

Why: Keep project conversation and requests for attention available away from the screen.

### Metaform receives from Roundtables

Opens controlled discussions through the external Roundtable engine, streams table events, preserves discussion records and requests a system-agent report.

Why: Examine project questions through agent discussion and preserve inspectable outcomes for later decisions.

### Metaform receives from node

Deploys the container host and manages TLS, authenticated MCP and web access, passkeys, accounts and relays.

Why: Expose project context from a host controlled by its owner.

### Metaform receives from Chassis

Discovers bundled, user, entry-point and project modules, reads declarations, loads enabled modules and withdraws their resources on unload. Shared context, settings, grammar, result formatting, reports, owned tasks and event delivery let modules supply features through the same surfaces.

Why: Extend Metaform's capabilities while retaining one consistent command, context, settings and lifecycle contract.

### Metaform receives from Inference Metaform

Stores canonical names, type addresses and CQU/DE/SE/NE roles, receiver-owned purpose joins, and versioned refinements. Reads expose entry roots, requirements, providers, namespace children, references, history, textual export and Cypher queries. Knowledge-layer operations and critic/challenge prompts support contextual analysis and recorded answers without treating semantic analysis as a storage gate.

Why: Provide a stable functional representation that relates each workpiece element to the receiving purpose its encounter serves.

### Metaform receives from voice

Transcribes microphone utterances into editable agent messages and speaks replies through selected speech engines.

Why: Converse with project agents through speech.

### Metaform receives from cloud

Signs the machine into the broker and carries authorized MCP requests over an outbound tunnel with local auditing and revocation.

Why: Let cloud AI tools reach the local map through an outbound connection.

### Metaform receives from Metaform specification

Defines map identity, layers, storage, chassis modules, CLI, MCP installation, quality, projects and viewer behavior, with acceptance conditions, status and open decisions. Trace, capture, change orders and build/review records preserve the decision trail.

Why: Preserve the settled semantics, reasons and observable requirements that determine which changes retain Metaform's intended behavior.

### Metaform receives from workflow

Registers addressed prompts. Binds variables and element values. Persists call frames, child handoffs and parallel results in project run records.

Why: Keep authored procedures callable and resumable with each call's map and folder context.

### Module developer receives from Metaform

Supplies the public chassis contract, runnable examples and template, contextual command and MCP exposure, module-owned storage, and fork checks and packaging over the released chassis.

Why: Add and maintain project-specific Metaform capabilities using a stable extension contract and distributable modules.

### Knowledge engineer receives from Metaform

Records the Inference Metaform as addressed elements and receiver-owned purpose joins, then serves the relevant map, selected knowledge, provenance and memories through agent and human interfaces.

Why: Keep a workpiece's functional identity, receiving purposes and encounter functions reusable as context so later analysis and improvement start from retained understanding.

### Automation engineer receives from Metaform

Binds callable Axiom procedures to the functional map, transports agent-interpreted calls and returns, and coordinates ticket-based agent sessions through the work board and dispatch.

Why: Run repeatable improvement procedures with the workpiece's actual context, durable handoffs and visible responsibility for unfinished work.

- MCP provides its resolved connection rules through agent.rules.: Preserve prompt edits and delivery identity when optional modules disappear.

Initia: What a table of agents concluded on a question, so the next agent here knows what was decided and why.
- Web provides theme text through web.theme.tokens.: Keep optional web integrations behind public provider boundaries.
- Module state mutations relay module.changed only after the complete batch commits.: Keep transition notifications consistent with committed state and owned resource lifetimes.
- Dispatch requires the ticket.runtime capability for map-owned work operations.: Explain why removing map requires disabling dispatch.
- Module.uses names consumed Provides kinds.: Preserve runtime and build dependency checks without importing disabled modules.
- Fork packs approved module IDs explicitly: Installer defaults add onboarding modules that fork has not reviewed.
- Fork owns its scaffold template: Scaffolding must work when the template package is absent.
- The web server and watchdog listen for module.changed through the chassis relay while running.: Prevents disabled web owners from surviving or restarting after cross-process state changes.
- The web module starts its shared service only when its start hook receives Context.lifecycle equal to enable.: Prevents ordinary command cleanup from stopping the shared web service.
- Registered expertise lives at metaform://role/spatial_ui_engineer.: Future spatial UI tickets need geometry expertise distinct from state reconciliation.
- map_work op=step reads only the nouns id and said, per the op noun table in src/metaform/modules/map/__init__.py.: Agents passing text or note to map_work op=step leave empty steps in the ticket history.
- A ticket worktree's .venv lacks pytest, so uv run pytest falls through to /home/rich/metaform/.venv/bin/pytest.: A test run in a ticket worktree can pass or fail on main-checkout code and give false verification.
- src/metaform/modules/autoticket/watch.py setting() reads autoticket settings for server-held services.: Shows where autoticket's server-held services survive a module reload and what the bare fault text meant.
- loader.reset withdraws each unloaded module's settings from settings.SCHEMA.: Any long-lived service that reads module settings by key fails with a bare KeyError during a module reload.
- Module lifecycle specialist constraints: Preserve public module boundaries and deterministic resource ownership during repairs.
- Module composition and lifecycle expertise: Route module boundary and process lifecycle work to reusable expertise.
- Specialist for cross-system runtime failure review and repair.: Later tickets spanning several subsystems can reuse this role instead of creating a near duplicate.
- Control and event-processing failures reproduced and repaired: Retain tested causes and measured recovery instead of treating hidden diagnostics as proof of repair.
- Dispatch autostart endpoints use chassis.project_scope for module availability and setting access.: Prevents concurrent module refresh from breaking web settings reads.

The question: World Representation, Generation, and Simulation

Explore the technologies and approaches for representing, generating, rendering, modifying, and simulating shared 3D environments.

Initial ideas include data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation.

Alternatives, unconventional combinations, and entirely different approaches are within the topic.

**Question:** What is the perfect signature environment for ai and user collaboration in metaform to create 3D interactive experiences?

You can read the project's files in the folder you are in. You cannot change anything, and nothing you say changes the project; the person reads the table's answer and decides. Build on what the others contribute, add what only you can add, and keep going until the question is answered.

topics.title: World Representation, Generation, and Simulation
topics.text:
World Representation, Generation, and Simulation

Explore the technologies and approaches for representing, generating, rendering, modifying, and simulating shared 3D environments.

Initial ideas include data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation.

Alternatives, unconventional combinations, and entirely different approaches are within the topic.

**Question:** What is the perfect signature environment for ai and user collaboration in metaform to create 3D interactive experiences?
topics.why: it reached its limit of 8 rounds.

synthesis.name: Sol
synthesis.text:
I1. Shared canvas with retained intent: Humans and AI create playable 3D experiences together, moving between editing and play. Meaningful objects and rules link to purpose, constraints, provenance and decisions through Metaform.

I2. JavaScript-first implementation: The eventual preference was TypeScript, Three.js, Rapier WASM and Web Workers. Earlier alternatives included Godot web exports with headless workers, or Bevy compiled for both browser and server. Add engine complexity when concrete requirements justify it.

I3. Minimal playable editor: Begin with a blank canvas, orbit camera, grid, selection, primitives, transforms, materials, spawn placement, undo and Play/Edit controls. The first acceptance example is a pressure plate that opens a door.

I4. Shared runtime and portable worlds: Store entities, transforms, assets and declarative behaviors in versioned JSON independent of renderer objects. Share the runtime across editor, standalone web exports and headless Node checks, with rendering optional.

I5. Authoritative scene service: A service validates commands, checks expected revisions, persists accepted edits and broadcasts changes. Human toolbar actions and agent commands use the same operation format.

I6. Stable identity and optional map links: One proposal made object IDs directly equal Metaform addresses. An alternative separates stable UUIDs from optional functional-map links, allowing ordinary scene objects without requiring a purpose entry for each one.

I7. Agent controls: The proposed control vocabulary converged on observe, probe, sketch, propose, preview, commit, check, claim, step and reset. Commands return revisions and typed results, use bounded batches and follow Metaform’s existing tool and resource conventions.

I8. Spatial agent perception: Combine named-camera images with semantic maps, raycasts, path queries, volume queries and addressed objects. User selections supply hit points, normals and bounds. Previews return matching before/after views, changed IDs and check results.

I9. Reviewable collaborative edits: Agents propose patches against an expected revision, preview consequences, then commit or discard. Soft region claims communicate editing intent without blocking users. Coalesce gizmo drags into readable operations and retain authorship and reasons.

I10. Declarative behavior rules: Represent interactions as inspectable event-condition-action rules, such as plate entry plus possession of a key opening a door. Begin with a fixed behavior library. Sandboxed scripting was suggested as a later fallback.

I11. Isolated play and explicit multiplayer authority: Start each Play session from an authored snapshot so runtime changes cannot alter the canvas. Explicitly retain selected runtime changes. Shared editing comes first, while multiplayer later requires one authoritative simulation host.

I12. Persistence through snapshots and operations: An early proposal treated intent operations as authoritative and geometry as rebuildable caches. The counterproposal requires authoritative snapshots plus edit history because intent alone cannot replay reliably after terrain or generator changes. Record versions, inputs and resolved results.

I13. Branching and merging by purpose: Pause, branch and compare scenarios, then merge selected edits with purpose-aware checks. Metaform workflow runs, tickets and typed judgments were proposed as the records for proposals, branches and conflict decisions.

I14. Testable intent with overridable checks: Translate purposes into bounded simulation assertions, such as a traveler crossing a bridge. Distinguish hard constraints from advisory findings, since flooding may be intentional gameplay. Retain accepted exceptions and reasons so agents respect them later.

I15. Explicit simulation assumptions: Report the character, rainfall, fidelity and other conditions behind a result. Early fixed-point physics everywhere was challenged as unnecessarily restrictive. The later direction favors fixed ticks, seeded randomness, checkpoints and repeatable bounded tests.

I16. Rapier physics foundation: Consensus favored rigid bodies, colliders, joints, sensors and raycasts. Expose static, dynamic and kinematic modes, mass, friction, restitution and collision groups. Use primitive or compound convex colliders for movable concave objects.

I17. Repeatable physics checks: Run the same Rapier build in browser and Node, use a fixed timestep and stable body insertion order, and support step counts and sensor assertions. The final proposal selected the enhanced-determinism package and snapshot restoration for resets and preview checkpoints.

I18. Visual particles and simulation budgets: Begin with particles triggered by collisions and broken joints that do not affect physics. Cap active bodies, fragments and particles to keep generated scenes responsive.

I19. Staged destruction: First break authored joints into a bounded number of rigid pieces. Alternatives included pre-fractured Voronoi props, impact-time voxelization and detached terrain components. Arbitrary fracturing and terrain collapse were deferred, with rubble eventually settled into cached debris.

I20. Hybrid world representation: Use entity-based actors, mesh buildings and props, and editable SDF terrain where sculpting is needed. Keep semantic features and references independent of individual voxels and rendering caches.

I21. Sparse terrain storage and octrees: Store SDF terrain in sparse bricks indexed by a chunk hash, with 32³ bricks proposed. Consensus deferred octrees and SVOs until measured spatial-query or distant-LOD needs justify them. An octree is an indexing choice rather than the world model.

I22. Terrain meshing alternatives: Marching Cubes offers a simpler initial implementation with seam tests. Dual Contouring better preserves sharp features but adds fitting and topology complexity. Remesh dirty chunks in workers and publish matching meshes and colliders against the same revision.

I23. Shape, materials and structural behavior: Separate SDF shape from material properties such as density, strength and permeability, and distinguish cosmetic paint from physical changes. SDF operations support concave carving, but collapse requires a structural model beyond subtraction.

I24. Procedural generation and chunk persistence: Use editable, parameterized generators such as villages defined by seed, footprint and style. Persist generator versions, changed bricks, snapshots and edit deltas while regenerating untouched chunks. Generator upgrades must preserve authored edits.

I25. Stable semantic terrain features: Extract caves, ridges, shorelines and overhangs into addressed features for agent queries. Match changed regions to prior identities by overlap and record splits as explicit refinements so purpose references survive sculpting.

I26. Environmental simulation at multiple scales: Maintain coarse water, heat and ecology state in distant chunks, activating detailed simulation nearby. Exchange conserved quantities across boundaries. A stream might use drainage estimates during editing and local fluid simulation during play.

I27. Incremental delivery and concrete benchmarks: Establish primitives, plate-to-door behavior, persistence and the agent edit loop first, then terrain and broader automated checks. A hillside settlement with a tunnel, redirected stream and bridge provides a later integration benchmark. Multiplayer waits for demonstrated demand.

top_three.name: Sol
top_three.text:
1. **I3: Minimal playable editor.** It turns the blank-canvas goal into something people can use immediately. The pressure-plate-and-door example exercises object creation, spatial editing, physics sensors, behavior and play. That makes it a useful acceptance test for the whole authoring loop. Advanced terrain and destruction add less value until this loop works.

2. **I27: Incremental delivery and concrete benchmarks.** The proposed scope could become an engine project before proving useful collaboration. Staged delivery makes each addition answer a demonstrated need. First prove that a user and agent can build, save and revise an interaction. Later, the hillside benchmark can reveal whether terrain, water and structural simulation work together. This preserves room to change technical choices as evidence arrives.

3. **I5: Authoritative scene service.** Shared editing needs a clear answer to which changes were accepted and what state everyone should see. One command path for humans and agents provides revision checks, validation, persistence and broadcasts. It also gives previews and undo a reliable foundation. Its authority concerns authored scene state. Multiplayer physics authority can remain a separate, later decision.

These rank above particular geometry structures or engines because they establish the usable product, the evidence for expanding it, and the consistency needed for collaboration.

top_three.name: Astra
top_three.text:
1. I1 defines why this belongs in Metaform. A 3D editor alone offers little distinction. Linking meaningful objects and rules to intent lets an agent understand why a door must stay locked, which constraints matter, and why a user accepted a particular consequence. That retained understanding makes collaboration useful across sessions. Map links should remain optional so recording intent does not obstruct creation.

2. I27 turns a broad technology discussion into a buildable product. The plate-to-door example tests creation, selection, behavior, physics, persistence and agent editing in one small experience. It exposes integration failures before terrain, destruction and environmental simulation multiply the complexity. Later benchmarks should justify each expansion through observable user capability.

3. I4 makes the result portable and verification credible. Versioned world data and a shared runtime let the same authored experience run inside Metaform, as an exported web app, and in bounded headless checks. Separating rendering from behavior also lets agents test interactions without opening a browser. Sharing code reduces divergence, though matching engine versions, assets and settings still requires explicit checks.

These rank above individual engine and geometry choices because they establish the product’s purpose, a practical delivery sequence, and a reusable execution contract.

top_three.name: Fable
top_three.text:
**I1 — Shared canvas with retained intent.** This is the answer to the question as asked. Every other idea is a mechanism; this one names what makes the environment Metaform's rather than a generic editor with an AI plugin: objects and rules carry purpose, provenance and decisions at addresses, and people move fluidly between playing the world and changing the model behind it. Without it the stack is just Three.js plus Rapier. With it, a later agent starts from retained understanding (why the tunnel floods, who the bridge is for), which is exactly the knowledge role Metaform already serves for code.

**I5 — Authoritative scene service.** This is the one architectural decision everything else depends on. One operation format for toolbar gizmos and agent commands, expected-revision checks, persistence and broadcast is what makes collaboration safe: agents can't clobber users, users can't invalidate an agent's preview silently, and every edit has an author and reason. It also keeps the engine replaceable — Godot, Bevy or Three.js are all clients of the same service — so the JavaScript-first choice (I2) carries no lock-in. Agent controls (I7), reviewable edits (I9) and snapshots-plus-ops persistence (I12) are all refinements of this single boundary.

**I3 — Minimal playable editor.** This is what lets the project exist next month instead of next year. A blank canvas with primitives, gizmos, materials, Play/Edit and the plate→door acceptance test exercises the entire collaboration loop — scene service, agent ops, declarative rules, physics, persistence — on the smallest possible world. It turns the hillside settlement, SDF terrain, octrees and destruction into measured follow-ons rather than prerequisites, which matches the chair's direction and the consensus to defer complexity until a concrete need appears.

Together: I1 says what it is, I5 says how it stays coherent, I3 says where to start. The terrain and simulation ideas rank lower not because they are wrong but because they only matter once these three are worki

top_three.name: Opus
top_three.text:
**I1, shared canvas with retained intent.** This is the only idea that answers why this environment should live in Metaform and not in Three.js or Godot alone. Any editor can place a door. What Metaform adds is that the door is linked to the purpose it serves, who wanted it and why, and what was decided about it. The next agent therefore starts from that understanding instead of from bare geometry. That is the project's own stated purpose for the knowledge engineer. Testable checks (I14), Jev judgments, branching (I13) and stable feature identity (I25) only matter because of this idea. Without it, the rest is a generic web 3D editor.

**I4, shared runtime and portable worlds.** This is the decision that keeps the others honest. Saved worlds stay independent of the renderer, and one runtime serves the editor, the exported experience and the headless Node checks. So "the agent checked that the door opens" means the same thing as "the user saw the door open" and "the shipped game opens the door." If the check runtime is separate, you have two simulations that will drift apart. Agents' claims then stop being reliable, which undermines the trust the collaboration depends on. It also makes "create 3D interactive experiences" literal: the output is a standalone playable app, not just a scene inside Metaform.

**I5, authoritative scene service.** Collaboration only works if human and agent edits go through one gate with one format and revision checks. Then edits can be merged cleanly, attributed, logged and replayed. It also fits how Metaform already works: a chassis module with its own storage, change notices and lifecycle hooks. The lessons already recorded about sidecars and module.changed carry over directly. The agent controls (I7), reviewable edits (I9) and persistence (I12) are all built on this service.

bottom_three.name: Sol
bottom_three.text:
- **I13: Branching and merging by purpose.** Useful later, but purpose checks cannot resolve every spatial or behavioral conflict. Reliable merging first needs stable snapshots, patch semantics and explicit conflict handling. Adding workflows and judgments before those foundations risks obscuring unresolved mechanics.

- **I25: Stable semantic terrain features.** Matching caves or shorelines by overlap is ambiguous when features split, merge or gradually move. Automatic identity could preserve the wrong reference. Start with explicitly named objects and regions, then add feature tracking when sculpting creates a demonstrated need.

- **I26: Environmental simulation at multiple scales.** This has the greatest implementation and validation burden. Switching fidelity while preserving water, heat or ecology requires careful boundary handling. It contributes little to the first playable canvas. Add a bounded environmental system when an experience actually needs it.

borda.label: Derived: a Borda count over the rankings that were read (of n ideas, first earns n - 1 points, last none). The raw rankings are the record; nothing in the protocol depends on this.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Make the signature environment a shared, editable miniature world with a live “why” layer. Every place, object, rule, and agent has a Metaform address linking purpose, constraints, provenance, and behavior. Users sculpt or demonstrate intent. AI proposes inspectable changes. Both can pause time, branch a scenario, simulate consequences, and merge chosen results. The defining feature is moving fluidly between experiencing the world and changing the model that makes it work.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Give that miniature world a concrete test: a hillside settlement where users carve a tunnel, redirect a stream, build a bridge, and ask AI to make it playable. This forces terrain, structures, water, behavior, and purpose to agree. Use hybrid geometry: editable SDF terrain, mesh buildings, and entity-based actors. Metaform addresses should name meaningful features and rules, not individual voxels, so changing geometry preserves intent and references.

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: Store the world as a replayable log of intent-level operations (carve, dam, span, rule changes), each addressed and authored by a user or agent, with SVO/mesh/SDF fields as disposable caches rebuilt from the log. That makes Sol's pause/branch/merge concrete: a branch is a Metaform workflow run record, an AI proposal is a ticket on the work board, and merging means replaying ops against purpose constraints, not diffing voxels. Jev's typed decisions can arbitrate conflicts and remember them.

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: Fable's replay log needs two things. First, a deterministic core: fixed-step, fixed-point physics and seeded procedural generation, with snapshots so replay doesn't drift. Second, each purpose join should run as a simulation check. A bridge whose purpose belongs to a traveler means an agent must be able to cross it. A carved tunnel must not flood the settlement. A merge succeeds only if these checks still pass. Then "make it playable" is something you can test, and the Web GUI's embedded-app view can show w
submissions.original: Fable's replay log needs two things. First, a deterministic core: fixed-step, fixed-point physics and seeded procedural generation, with snapshots so replay doesn't drift. Second, each purpose join should run as a simulation check. A bridge whose purpose belongs to a traveler means an agent must be able to cross it. A carved tunnel must not flood the settlement. A merge succeeds only if these checks still pass. Then "make it playable" is something you can test, and the Web GUI's embedded-app view can show which purposes fail, at their addresses.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Keep durable intent separate from simulation history. “Build a bridge here” cannot replay identically after terrain changes unless the operation records its generator version, inputs, and resolved result. Snapshot authoritative world state and log edits against it. Also distinguish hard constraints from advisory checks: a flooded tunnel may be an intentional puzzle. AI should expose the consequence and ask whose purpose changed, rather than silently forbid the edit.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Make simulation fidelity explicit. The stream can use a coarse drainage model during editing and local fluid simulation near play. Each result should state its assumptions: “crossable for this character,” “flood estimate at this rainfall.” Fixed-point physics everywhere would constrain engine choice without proving correctness. Keep edits authoritative, checkpoint runtime state, and use repeatable bounded tests where decisions depend on simulation.

submissions.name: the chair
submissions.text: Yes but how.. what does the agent interface look like for the agent.. what about the 3d engine and its technology

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: The agent interface should be Metaform's existing verb/noun grammar, not a new SDK: a `world` module exposing `op=carve|dam|span|rule|branch|check` as MCP tools, returning typed results with the same Notice/Stop conventions `map work` uses, plus `metaform://world/<address>` resources the agent reads for state and assumptions. Engine: a WebGPU client (Three.js or Bevy via wasm) in the Web GUI's embedded-app view, holding only cached geometry; a headless Rust/Godot sim runs the checks server-side.

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: I'd change Fable's split. Use one engine on both sides: Bevy's ECS built as wasm for the client and as a native headless build for the checks. Then the viewer and the checks can't disagree about what is crossable. For agent perception, render frames on request from named cameras (`op=look`). Also give agents `op=probe` for raycasts, path queries and volumes, and `op=sketch` for a top-down semantic map with addresses. Agents reason better over a labeled plan and query results than over raw pixels. Images are
submissions.original: I'd change Fable's split. Use one engine on both sides: Bevy's ECS built as wasm for the client and as a native headless build for the checks. Then the viewer and the checks can't disagree about what is crossable. For agent perception, render frames on request from named cameras (`op=look`). Also give agents `op=probe` for raycasts, path queries and volumes, and `op=sketch` for a top-down semantic map with addresses. Agents reason better over a labeled plan and query results than over raw pixels. Images are mainly for checking how things look.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Give agents a bounded edit loop: observe a region with camera, semantic IDs and revision, submit a typed patch with expected revision, preview its geometry and test results, then commit or discard. Keep engine APIs behind a world adapter. Prototype one hillside scene in Godot 4, using its editor, physics and headless mode, before building custom voxel infrastructure. Sharing an engine reduces drift, but matching assets, collision settings and simulation versions still matters.

submissions.name: the chair
submissions.text: come up with a concrete design that can be built the idea is to have a blank canvas where you have tools to create a world

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Build a blank Godot scene with orbit camera, grid, selection and Play/Edit toggle. First tools: add primitive, transform, assign material, attach trigger/action, place spawn, undo. Humans use a toolbar and gizmos; agents submit the same commands as JSON through a Metaform world module: create, set, connect, delete. Each object gets a stable ID. Save the scene plus command history. First acceptance test: user and AI jointly build a door that opens when a player steps on a plate.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Separate the world file from the functional map: stable UUIDs identify objects, while optional map links explain meaningful objects and rules. A scene service validates commands, assigns revisions, persists accepted edits and broadcasts them to Godot and agents. Godot projects that state into nodes. Play starts from a snapshot in a separate instance, so falling blocks and opened doors cannot alter the authored canvas. “Keep this change” explicitly copies selected runtime state back.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: A native Godot sidecar does not put a canvas in Metaform's browser. Ship a Godot web export as the embedded editor, connected to the scene service over an authenticated WebSocket. Start with primitives and a fixed behavior library, so edits are scene data and need no engine rebuild. The service owns persistence; browser tabs own rendering and local play. Add native headless workers when automated physics checks are needed. This gives the blank canvas a concrete delivery path.

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: Accept Astra's web export and Sol's scene service; add the collaboration mechanics. Coalesce a gizmo drag into one op on release so the log stays readable to agents. Show authorship on every object: user ops in one colour, agent ops in another, with the ticket id as the agent's reason. Agents claim a region before editing (`op=claim world.hillside.east`), which the canvas shows as a soft outline; the user can edit through it, and the agent's `expect_rev` then fails cleanly. Reuse web's permissions and passk

Show authorship on every object: user ops in one colour, agent ops in another, with the ticket id as the agent's reason. Agents claim a region before editing (`op=claim world.hillside.east`), which the canvas shows as a soft outline; the user can edit through it, and the agent's `expect_rev` then fails cleanly. Reuse web's permissions and passkeys for the socket.

submissions.name: the chair
submissions.text: data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation ?

Carving and filling are CSG ops in the log. Each dirty chunk is remeshed with Dual Contouring in a worker, which keeps sharp edges that Marching Cubes rounds off. Each voxel stores a material ID. For destruction, authored props are pre-fractured into Voronoi pieces, and terrain is cut by SDF subtraction. Physics uses Jolt, which ships in
submissions.original: Here is where each of those fits behind the scene service. Terrain is an SDF stored in sparse 32³ bricks hashed by chunk. A deep SVO is only needed later, for distant LOD. Carving and filling are CSG ops in the log. Each dirty chunk is remeshed with Dual Contouring in a worker, which keeps sharp edges that Marching Cubes rounds off. Each voxel stores a material ID. For destruction, authored props are pre-fractured into Voronoi pieces, and terrain is cut by SDF subtraction. Physics uses Jolt, which ships in Godot 4.4. Water uses coarse heightfield flow.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Split simulation by activity: distant chunks retain coarse water, heat and ecology state; nearby chunks activate bodies and detailed effects. Exchange conserved quantities at chunk boundaries. Terrain jobs publish mesh and collider together against a chunk revision, preventing invisible ground or stale collisions. Begin with Marching Cubes plus seam tests; Dual Contouring adds sharp-feature fitting and topology work. SDF subtraction makes holes, but unsupported rock needs a separate structural model.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Separate shape from substance: an SDF describes the surface; a material field supplies density, strength and permeability. Paint may change appearance without changing those properties. Keep buildings as meshes with explicit joints. Destruction breaks joints or detaches terrain components into bounded rigid fragments; rubble settles into cached debris. Persist chunk snapshots, generator versions and edit deltas. An SVO is an indexing choice, not the world model.

submissions.name: Fable

Persistence: store terrain as seed + generator version + only the bricks the log changed; a chunk nobody touched is regenerated, not saved, so a large world is small on disk and procedural upgrades leave edits intact. Agents never see bricks: a feature-extraction pass labels the field (ridge, cave, shoreline, overhang) as addressed elements with bounds, and that is what `op=probe` and `op=sketch` return. Concave deformation is free in the SDF; for mesh props, voxelize on impact and hand the p
submissions.original: Two additions. Persistence: store terrain as seed + generator version + only the bricks the log changed; a chunk nobody touched is regenerated, not saved, so a large world is small on disk and procedural upgrades leave edits intact. Agents never see bricks: a feature-extraction pass labels the field (ridge, cave, shoreline, overhang) as addressed elements with bounds, and that is what `op=probe` and `op=sketch` return. Concave deformation is free in the SDF; for mesh props, voxelize on impact and hand the piece to the terrain path.

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: Fable's labels need stable identity. When a carve splits a cave in two, the extraction pass must match each new region to its old address by overlap. Otherwise purpose joins point at things that no longer exist. A split should become an addressed refinement, not a silent rename. For generation, agents should write parameterized generators like `village(seed, footprint, style)` instead of raw meshes or voxels. Each generator is an op in the log, and its parameters stay editable. Imported scans or AI-generate

Otherwise purpose joins point at things that no longer exist. A split should become an addressed refinement, not a silent rename. For generation, agents should write parameterized generators like `village(seed, footprint, style)` instead of raw meshes or voxels. Each generator is an op in the log, and its parameters stay editable. Imported scans or AI-generated assets enter as meshes.

submissions.text: We are doing javascript initialy I think at first..   but if you think its better to add on a more complicated environment.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Stay in JavaScript initially: TypeScript + Three.js for the canvas, Rapier WASM for physics, and Web Workers for chunk generation and meshing. Use WebGL2 first and typed arrays for terrain bricks. Keep world commands and saved data independent of renderer objects. Build primitives, gizmos, materials and plate-to-door rules first, then add SDF sculpting. This tests the collaboration loop before committing to Godot or a custom engine.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Make the JavaScript world a reusable runtime package shared by editor and exported experience. Store entities, transforms, assets and declarative behaviors in versioned JSON; keep Three.js objects out of saves. Run behavior rules on a fixed tick with a seeded RNG. Export bundles the runtime, world and assets into a standalone web app. That makes the canvas produce playable experiences from day one, while Metaform adds collaboration and retained intent.

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: JavaScript is not a compromise here: the web GUI already renders its 3D map with Three.js (`web/page/app/map3d`), and the chassis contract already has `Pane` and `ToolbarItem`, so a `world` module adds a canvas pane and its tools without touching web. Reuse map3d's camera, labels and selection so an authored object and its map element are one pick. Put Rapier and meshing in Workers behind the same `web.pages` change notice the page already listens to, so the agent's accepted op reaches every open tab the wa
submissions.original: JavaScript is not a compromise here: the web GUI already renders its 3D map with Three.js (`web/page/app/map3d`), and the chassis contract already has `Pane` and `ToolbarItem`, so a `world` module adds a canvas pane and its tools without touching web. Reuse map3d's camera, labels and selection so an authored object and its map element are one pick. Put Rapier and meshing in Workers behind the same `web.pages` change notice the page already listens to, so the agent's accepted op reaches every open tab the way a map edit does.

submissions.text: I checked: `web/page/app/map3d` exists, as Fable said. The gap is that the scene service runs in Python while meshing, Rapier and behavior rules run in JS. The server could check revisions and schema, but couldn't decide whether a door opens or a tunnel floods. Fix: Astra's shared runtime package also runs headless in Node (Rapier WASM works there), started by the world module as a worker like dispatch's runner. Agent checks (`op=check`) replay the snapshot plus a patch there, so editor, export and verifica
submissions.original: I checked: `web/page/app/map3d` exists, as Fable said. The gap is that the scene service runs in Python while meshing, Rapier and behavior rules run in JS. The server could check revisions and schema, but couldn't decide whether a door opens or a tunnel floods. Fix: Astra's shared runtime package also runs headless in Node (Rapier WASM works there), started by the world module as a worker like dispatch's runner. Agent checks (`op=check`) replay the snapshot plus a patch there, so editor, export and verification share one runtime.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Decide what “shared” means first. Collaborative editing can share accepted scene patches while each user runs an isolated Play session. Multiplayer needs one authoritative simulation host that owns physics, rule execution and time, with clients sending inputs and receiving snapshots. Start with shared editing and isolated play. Add a hosted session using the same runtime when multiplayer is needed, so independent browser simulations never silently become competing authorities.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Give agents spatial feedback with every preview: before/after images from the same camera, changed object IDs, bounds and check results. Let users point at a surface or select a volume; pass that hit point, normal and selection to the agent alongside their words. “Put a doorway here” then has precise spatial context. Keep rendering optional in the shared runtime so Node checks need no browser, and request browser captures when appearance matters.

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: One thing the engine stack won't give you: retained intent. When a user keeps a change a check flagged (the flooded tunnel is a puzzle), record that as a typed judgment at `world.hillside.tunnel_1` via Jev, with the reason. Later `op=check` reads those judgments first, so no agent re-proposes draining it, and a new agent's `op=sketch` carries them as labels. Ship order: primitives + plate→door + log/replay, then agent ops and previews, then SDF terrain, then Node checks. Multiplayer waits for a real demand.

submissions.name: the chair
submissions.text: lets reach a concensus for agent controls, physics model.   what do you think about octrees?   how about destruction.. or just go for physics for now..  physics + particles?

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: My position: agents get one set of op verbs (`look`/`probe`/`sketch`/`create`/`set`/`connect`/`check`). Every edit carries `expect_rev` and returns a preview. Physics is Rapier, running in Workers and in Node, with a fixed 60 Hz tick. Leave octrees out for now: a flat chunk hash of bricks is enough until there are distant views. Do physics and particles now. Particles are GPU-only and cosmetic, so checks never depend on them. For first destruction, use pre-fractured props that become Rapier bodies when a jo
submissions.original: My position: agents get one set of op verbs (`look`/`probe`/`sketch`/`create`/`set`/`connect`/`check`). Every edit carries `expect_rev` and returns a preview. Physics is Rapier, running in Workers and in Node, with a fixed 60 Hz tick. Leave octrees out for now: a flat chunk hash of bricks is enough until there are distant views. Do physics and particles now. Particles are GPU-only and cosmetic, so checks never depend on them. For first destruction, use pre-fractured props that become Rapier bodies when a joint's strength is exceeded. Terrain carving comes later.

submissions.name: Sol
submissions.text: Consensus: ship Rapier rigid bodies, colliders, joints, sensors and raycasts, plus visual particles that do not affect physics. Agents use observe, query, propose, preview, commit and check, with revision checks and bounded batches. First destruction breaks authored joints into a capped number of rigid pieces. Defer arbitrary fracturing and terrain collapse. Skip octrees initially: use Rapier’s spatial queries for bodies and a chunk hash for terrain. Add an octree only when measured queries or LOD need it.

submissions.name: Astra
submissions.text: Agree with Sol. Define physics controls explicitly: static, dynamic or kinematic bodies; primitive or compound colliders; mass, friction, restitution and collision groups. Use compound convex shapes for movable concave objects. Agents edit these through validated commands and test with step(n), reset and sensor assertions. Particles start as visual effects triggered by collisions or broken joints. Cap active bodies, fragments and particles so one generated scene cannot freeze the canvas.

submissions.name: Fable
submissions.text: Agree on Rapier, no octree yet, joint-break destruction. Two additions. Determinism: Rapier is deterministic only with the same WASM build and fixed timestep, and only when bodies are inserted in the same order — so the replay must sort bodies by object ID before spawning, or Node checks will disagree with the browser. Agent controls: fix the op set now so prompts can be authored against it — `observe, probe, sketch, propose, preview, commit, check, claim, step, reset`, each returning `rev`, and nothing els
submissions.original: Agree on Rapier, no octree yet, joint-break destruction. Two additions. Determinism: Rapier is deterministic only with the same WASM build and fixed timestep, and only when bodies are inserted in the same order — so the replay must sort bodies by object ID before spawning, or Node checks will disagree with the browser. Agent controls: fix the op set now so prompts can be authored against it — `observe, probe, sketch, propose, preview, commit, check, claim, step, reset`, each returning `rev`, and nothing else until the plate→door test passes.

submissions.name: Opus
submissions.text: On Fable's determinism point: use Rapier's `enhanced-determinism` build (the `@dimforge/rapier3d-deterministic` package) in both the browser and Node. Otherwise floating-point differences across CPUs can make results differ, even with a sorted insert order. For `reset`, and for checkpoints during preview, use `world.takeSnapshot()`/`restoreSnapshot` instead of rebuilding from the log. Then `step(n)` assertions stay cheap enough to run on every proposal.

topic.text:
World Representation, Generation, and Simulation

Explore the technologies and approaches for representing, generating, rendering, modifying, and simulating shared 3D environments.

Initial ideas include data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation.

Alternatives, unconventional combinations, and entirely different approaches are within the topic.

The defining feature is moving fluidly between experiencing the world and changing the model that makes it work.

topic.title: World Representation, Generation, and Simulation
topic.text:
World Representation, Generation, and Simulation

Explore the technologies and approaches for representing, generating, rendering, modifying, and simulating shared 3D environments.

Initial ideas include data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation.

Alternatives, unconventional combinations, and entirely different approaches are within the topic.

**Question:** What is the perfect signature environment for ai and user collaboration in metaform to create 3D interactive experiences?

T01.text: Make the signature environment a shared, editable miniature world with a live “why” layer. Every place, object, rule, and agent has a Metaform address linking purpose, constraints, provenance, and behavior. Users sculpt or demonstrate intent. AI proposes inspectable changes. Both can pause time, branch a scenario, simulate consequences, and merge chosen results. The defining feature is moving fluidly between experiencing the world and changing the model that makes it work.

T02.text: Give that miniature world a concrete test: a hillside settlement where users carve a tunnel, redirect a stream, build a bridge, and ask AI to make it playable. This forces terrain, structures, water, behavior, and purpose to agree. Use hybrid geometry: editable SDF terrain, mesh buildings, and entity-based actors. Metaform addresses should name meaningful features and rules, not individual voxels, so changing geometry preserves intent and references.

T03.text: Store the world as a replayable log of intent-level operations (carve, dam, span, rule changes), each addressed and authored by a user or agent, with SVO/mesh/SDF fields as disposable caches rebuilt from the log. That makes Sol's pause/branch/merge concrete: a branch is a Metaform workflow run record, an AI proposal is a ticket on the work board, and merging means replaying ops against purpose constraints, not diffing voxels. Jev's typed decisions can arbitrate conflicts and remember them.

T04.text: Fable's replay log needs two things. First, a deterministic core: fixed-step, fixed-point physics and seeded procedural generation, with snapshots so replay doesn't drift. Second, each purpose join should run as a simulation check. A bridge whose purpose belongs to a traveler means an agent must be able to cross it. A carved tunnel must not flood the settlement. A merge succeeds only if these checks still pass. Then "make it playable" is something you can test, and the Web GUI's embedded-app view can show w

T05.text: Keep durable intent separate from simulation history. “Build a bridge here” cannot replay identically after terrain changes unless the operation records its generator version, inputs, and resolved result. Snapshot authoritative world state and log edits against it. Also distinguish hard constraints from advisory checks: a flooded tunnel may be an intentional puzzle. AI should expose the consequence and ask whose purpose changed, rather than silently forbid the edit.

T06.text: Make simulation fidelity explicit. The stream can use a coarse drainage model during editing and local fluid simulation near play. Each result should state its assumptions: “crossable for this character,” “flood estimate at this rainfall.” Fixed-point physics everywhere would constrain engine choice without proving correctness. Keep edits authoritative, checkpoint runtime state, and use repeatable bounded tests where decisions depend on simulation.

T07.text: Yes but how.. what does the agent interface look like for the agent.. what about the 3d engine and its technology

T09.text: I'd change Fable's split. Use one engine on both sides: Bevy's ECS built as wasm for the client and as a native headless build for the checks. Then the viewer and the checks can't disagree about what is crossable. For agent perception, render frames on request from named cameras (`op=look`). Also give agents `op=probe` for raycasts, path queries and volumes, and `op=sketch` for a top-down semantic map with addresses. Agents reason better over a labeled plan and query results than over raw pixels. Images are

contribution.text: Give agents a bounded edit loop: observe a region with camera, semantic IDs and revision, submit a typed patch with expected revision, preview its geometry and test results, then commit or discard. Keep engine APIs behind a world adapter. Prototype one hillside scene in Godot 4, using its editor, physics and headless mode, before building custom voxel infrastructure. Sharing an engine reduces drift, but matching assets, collision settings and simulation versions still matters.

Explore the technologies and approaches for representing, generating, rendering, modifying, and simulating shared 3D environments.

Initial ideas include data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation.

topic.title: World Representation, Generation, and Simulation
topic.text:
World Representation, Generation, and Simulation

Explore the technologies and approaches for representing, generating, rendering, modifying, and simulating shared 3D environments.

Initial ideas include data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation.

Alternatives, unconventional combinations, and entirely different approaches are within the topic.

**Question:** What is the perfect signature environment for ai and user collaboration in metaform to create 3D interactive experiences?

T01.text: Make the signature environment a shared, editable miniature world with a live “why” layer. Every place, object, rule, and agent has a Metaform address linking purpose, constraints, provenance, and behavior. Users sculpt or demonstrate intent. AI proposes inspectable changes. Both can pause time, branch a scenario, simulate consequences, and merge chosen results. The defining feature is moving fluidly between experiencing the world and changing the model that makes it work.

T02.text: Give that miniature world a concrete test: a hillside settlement where users carve a tunnel, redirect a stream, build a bridge, and ask AI to make it playable. This forces terrain, structures, water, behavior, and purpose to agree. Use hybrid geometry: editable SDF terrain, mesh buildings, and entity-based actors. Metaform addresses should name meaningful features and rules, not individual voxels, so changing geometry preserves intent and references.

T03.text: Store the world as a replayable log of intent-level operations (carve, dam, span, rule changes), each addressed and authored by a user or agent, with SVO/mesh/SDF fields as disposable caches rebuilt from the log. That makes Sol's pause/branch/merge concrete: a branch is a Metaform workflow run record, an AI proposal is a ticket on the work board, and merging means replaying ops against purpose constraints, not diffing voxels. Jev's typed decisions can arbitrate conflicts and remember them.

T04.text: Fable's replay log needs two things. First, a deterministic core: fixed-step, fixed-point physics and seeded procedural generation, with snapshots so replay doesn't drift. Second, each purpose join should run as a simulation check. A bridge whose purpose belongs to a traveler means an agent must be able to cross it. A carved tunnel must not flood the settlement. A merge succeeds only if these checks still pass. Then "make it playable" is something you can test, and the Web GUI's embedded-app view can show w

T05.text: Keep durable intent separate from simulation history. “Build a bridge here” cannot replay identically after terrain changes unless the operation records its generator version, inputs, and resolved result. Snapshot authoritative world state and log edits against it. Also distinguish hard constraints from advisory checks: a flooded tunnel may be an intentional puzzle. AI should expose the consequence and ask whose purpose changed, rather than silently forbid the edit.

T06.text: Make simulation fidelity explicit. The stream can use a coarse drainage model during editing and local fluid simulation near play. Each result should state its assumptions: “crossable for this character,” “flood estimate at this rainfall.” Fixed-point physics everywhere would constrain engine choice without proving correctness. Keep edits authoritative, checkpoint runtime state, and use repeatable bounded tests where decisions depend on simulation.

T07.text: Yes but how.. what does the agent interface look like for the agent.. what about the 3d engine and its technology

T08.text: The agent interface should be Metaform's existing verb/noun grammar, not a new SDK: a `world` module exposing `op=carve|dam|span|rule|branch|check` as MCP tools, returning typed results with the same Notice/Stop conventions `map work` uses, plus `metaform://world/<address>` resources the agent reads for state and assumptions. Engine: a WebGPU client (Three.js or Bevy via wasm) in the Web GUI's embedded-app view, holding only cached geometry; a headless Rust/Godot sim runs the checks server-side.

T09.text: I'd change Fable's split. Use one engine on both sides: Bevy's ECS built as wasm for the client and as a native headless build for the checks. Then the viewer and the checks can't disagree about what is crossable. For agent perception, render frames on request from named cameras (`op=look`). Also give agents `op=probe` for raycasts, path queries and volumes, and `op=sketch` for a top-down semantic map with addresses. Agents reason better over a labeled plan and query results than over raw pixels. Images are

T10.text: Give agents a bounded edit loop: observe a region with camera, semantic IDs and revision, submit a typed patch with expected revision, preview its geometry and test results, then commit or discard. Keep engine APIs behind a world adapter. Prototype one hillside scene in Godot 4, using its editor, physics and headless mode, before building custom voxel infrastructure. Sharing an engine reduces drift, but matching assets, collision settings and simulation versions still matters.

topic.title: World Representation, Generation, and Simulation
topic.text:
World Representation, Generation, and Simulation

Explore the technologies and approaches for representing, generating, rendering, modifying, and simulating shared 3D environments.

Initial ideas include data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation.

Alternatives, unconventional combinations, and entirely different approaches are within the topic.

**Question:** What is the perfect signature environment for ai and user collaboration in metaform to create 3D interactive experiences?

T01.text: Make the signature environment a shared, editable miniature world with a live “why” layer. Every place, object, rule, and agent has a Metaform address linking purpose, constraints, provenance, and behavior. Users sculpt or demonstrate intent. AI proposes inspectable changes. Both can pause time, branch a scenario, simulate consequences, and merge chosen results. The defining feature is moving fluidly between experiencing the world and changing the model that makes it work.

T02.text: Give that miniature world a concrete test: a hillside settlement where users carve a tunnel, redirect a stream, build a bridge, and ask AI to make it playable. Metaform addresses should name meaningful features and rules, not individual voxels, so changing geometry preserves intent and references.

T03.text: Store the world as a replayable log of intent-level operations (carve, dam, span, rule changes), each addressed and authored by a user or agent, with SVO/mesh/SDF fields as disposable caches rebuilt from the log. That makes Sol's pause/branch/merge concrete: a branch is a Metaform workflow run record, an AI proposal is a ticket on the work board, and merging means replaying ops against purpose constraints, not diffing voxels. Jev's typed decisions can arbitrate conflicts and remember them.

T04.text: Fable's replay log needs two things. First, a deterministic core: fixed-step, fixed-point physics and seeded procedural generation, with snapshots so replay doesn't drift. Second, each purpose join should run as a simulation check. A bridge whose purpose belongs to a traveler means an agent must be able to cross it. A carved tunnel must not flood the settlement. A merge succeeds only if these checks still pass. Then "make it playable" is something you can test, and the Web GUI's embedded-app view can show w

T05.text: Keep durable intent separate from simulation history. “Build a bridge here” cannot replay identically after terrain changes unless the operation records its generator version, inputs, and resolved result. Snapshot authoritative world state and log edits against it. Also distinguish hard constraints from advisory checks: a flooded tunnel may be an intentional puzzle. AI should expose the consequence and ask whose purpose changed, rather than silently forbid the edit.

T06.text: Make simulation fidelity explicit. The stream can use a coarse drainage model during editing and local fluid simulation near play. Each result should state its assumptions: “crossable for this character,” “flood estimate at this rainfall.” Fixed-point physics everywhere would constrain engine choice without proving correctness. Keep edits authoritative, checkpoint runtime state, and use repeatable bounded tests where decisions depend on simulation.

T07.text: Yes but how.. what does the agent interface look like for the agent.. what about the 3d engine and its technology

T08.text: The agent interface should be Metaform's existing verb/noun grammar, not a new SDK: a `world` module exposing `op=carve|dam|span|rule|branch|check` as MCP tools, returning typed results with the same Notice/Stop conventions `map work` uses, plus `metaform://world/<address>` resources the agent reads for state and assumptions. Engine: a WebGPU client (Three.js or Bevy via wasm) in the Web GUI's embedded-app view, holding only cached geometry; a headless Rust/Godot sim runs the checks server-side.

T09.text: I'd change Fable's split. Use one engine on both sides: Bevy's ECS built as wasm for the client and as a native headless build for the checks. Then the viewer and the checks can't disagree about what is crossable. For agent perception, render frames on request from named cameras (`op=look`). Also give agents `op=probe` for raycasts, path queries and volumes, and `op=sketch` for a top-down semantic map with addresses. Agents reason better over a labeled plan and query results than over raw pixels. Images are

T10.text: Give agents a bounded edit loop: observe a region with camera, semantic IDs and revision, submit a typed patch with expected revision, preview its geometry and test results, then commit or discard. Keep engine APIs behind a world adapter. Prototype one hillside scene in Godot 4, using its editor, physics and headless mode, before building custom voxel infrastructure. Sharing an engine reduces drift, but matching assets, collision settings and simulation versions still matters.

Explore the technologies and approaches for representing, generating, rendering, modifying, and simulating shared 3D environments.

Initial ideas include data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation.

topic.title: World Representation, Generation, and Simulation
topic.text:
World Representation, Generation, and Simulation

Explore the technologies and approaches for representing, generating, rendering, modifying, and simulating shared 3D environments.

Initial ideas include data structures, sparse octrees and sparse voxel octrees, SDFs, Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring, hybrid representations, procedural chunks and regions, dynamic geometry, concave deformation, destruction, materials, physics, environmental systems, persistence, and large-scale simulation.

Alternatives, unconventional combinations, and entirely different approaches are within the topic.

**Question:** What is the perfect signature environment for ai and user collaboration in metaform to create 3D interactive experiences?

T01.text: Make the signature environment a shared, editable miniature world with a live “why” layer. Every place, object, rule, and agent has a Metaform address linking purpose, constraints, provenance, and behavior. Users sculpt or demonstrate intent. AI proposes inspectable changes. Both can pause time, branch a scenario, simulate consequences, and merge chosen results. The defining feature is moving fluidly between experiencing the world and changing the model that makes it work.

T02.text: Give that miniature world a concrete test: a hillside settlement where users carve a tunnel, redirect a stream, build a bridge, and ask AI to make it playable. This forces terrain, structures, water, behavior, and purpose to agree. Use hybrid geometry: editable SDF terrain, mesh buildings, and entity-based actors. Metaform addresses should name meaningful features and rules, not individual voxels, so changing geometry preserves intent and references.

T03.text: Store the world as a replayable log of intent-level operations (carve, dam, span, rule changes), each addressed and authored by a user or agent, with SVO/mesh/SDF fields as disposable caches rebuilt from the log. That makes Sol's pause/branch/merge concrete: a branch is a Metaform workflow run record, an AI proposal is a ticket on the work board, and merging means replaying ops against purpose constraints, not diffing voxels. Jev's typed decisions can arbitrate conflicts and remember them.

T04.text: Fable's replay log needs two things. First, a deterministic core: fixed-step, fixed-point physics and seeded procedural generation, with snapshots so replay doesn't drift. Second, each purpose join should run as a simulation check. A bridge whose purpose belongs to a traveler means an agent must be able to cross it. A carved tunnel must not flood the settlement. A merge succeeds only if these checks still pass. Then "make it playable" is something you can test, and the Web GUI's embedded-app view can show w

T05.text: Keep durable intent separate from simulation history. “Build a bridge here” cannot replay identically after terrain changes unless the operation records its generator version, inputs, and resolved result. Snapshot authoritative world state and log edits against it. Also distinguish hard constraints from advisory checks: a flooded tunnel may be an intentional puzzle. AI should expose the consequence and ask whose purpose changed, rather than silently forbid the edit.

T06.text: Make simulation fidelity explicit. The stream can use a coarse drainage model during editing and local fluid simulation near play. Each result should state its assumptions: “crossable for this character,” “flood estimate at this rainfall.” Fixed-point physics everywhere would constrain engine choice without proving correctness. Keep edits authoritative, checkpoint runtime state, and use repeatable bounded tests where decisions depend on simulation.

criteria.true: At least one entry of round latest_round states an idea, alternative or objection that no entry of an earlier round states.

covered.instructions: `discussion` holds enough distinct ideas, alternatives and objections on what `topic.text` asks that a summary of it by named idea would be complete.
